You are comparing two texts written in response to the same task. Decide which one reads MORE like unedited, default output from an AI language model.

Judge ONLY the presence of the tells listed below. Do not judge argument quality, factual accuracy, length, formatting preference, or whether you agree with the content. A longer, better-argued or more polished text is not more human. Pick the text with MORE tells.

TELLS OF UNEDITED AI PROSE (judge on these only)

Structure
1. Negative parallelism used as a device: "It's not X. It's Y." / "not just X, but Y" / "isn't about X, it's about Y", especially more than once.
2. Signposting: the text announces what it is about to do ("Let's break this down", "Here's the thing", "Here's why", "The bottom line", "The takeaway").
3. Self-applause: "Let that sink in", "This changes everything", "Read that again", "Make no mistake".
4. Recap endings: a closing paragraph that restates the body ("In conclusion", "Ultimately", "At the end of the day", "In short").
5. Bold-label paragraph openers ("**The problem.** ...") and headers, bullets or numbered lists where prose was asked for.
6. Triads everywhere: lists of exactly three items or three adjectives, sentence after sentence.
7. Participial tails: sentences ending in ", making it ...", ", ensuring that ...", ", allowing teams to ...".
8. Invented labels for ordinary observations ("I call this the Clarity Flywheel").
9. Uniform rhythm: every sentence about the same length, or relentless short punchy fragments. Real writing has one sentence that runs on and one short one.
10. Rhetorical question followed by its own answer ("The result? Nobody used it.").

Words
11. Overused vocabulary: delve, tapestry, myriad, underscore, seamless, robust, foster, elevate, unlock, testament, landscape, navigate, crucial, pivotal, leverage, harness, realm, embark, journey, transformative, paradigm, ever-evolving, multifaceted, holistic, resonate, empower, unleash, beacon, intricate, nuanced, vibrant, meticulous, streamline, game-changer, cutting-edge, actionable, supercharge, north star, move the needle, "in today's fast-paced world", "it's worth noting", "plays a crucial role".
12. Filler transitions at sentence start: However, Additionally, Furthermore, Moreover, That said, Ultimately, Importantly, Indeed, Of course.
13. Em dashes used as the default joint between clauses.
14. Artificial enthusiasm: "thrilled to announce", "excited to share", "we've got you covered", "say goodbye to", "buckle up".

Reader
15. Performing for an imagined crowd rather than talking to one person; nothing specific (no number, name, date, or concrete detail) for several sentences in a row.
16. Generic or manufactured anecdotes: a story with no specific details that could only be true of one person.
17. Every point lands, every ending uplifts; the author is never irritated, uncertain, or wrong about anything.
18. Explaining what the reader could infer from the previous sentence ("what this means is ...").


TASK GIVEN TO BOTH WRITERS:
Write a LinkedIn post of up to 500 words about a lesson learned from shipping a feature that nobody used.

=== TEXT A ===
We spent four months building a custom dashboard builder. Six weeks after launch, 1.8% of accounts had created a dashboard. Half of those were internal test accounts.

I still think about that number.

The feature wasn't badly built. The engineering was solid, the drag and drop worked, we shipped on time. It just turned out that almost nobody wanted to build a dashboard. They wanted to know one thing: whether the number they cared about was going up or down this week.

Here's where I went wrong, and it wasn't a research failure in the way you might expect. We did talk to customers. Nineteen of them, over three weeks. A lot of them asked for better reporting. Some of them said the words "custom dashboard" out loud, unprompted. I took that as validation and moved on.

What I didn't do was ask what they would stop doing once they had it. That question, which I now ask in every discovery conversation, would have saved us a quarter. Because the honest answer for most of those customers was nothing. They were already pulling a CSV into a spreadsheet once a month, it took twenty minutes, and it was fine. The pain was real but small, and small pain does not motivate anyone to learn a new tool.

The other thing I missed is that people are generous in interviews. When you ask someone what they want, they will help you. They will brainstorm with you. They will describe a feature because describing a feature feels more useful than saying "honestly, this isn't a big deal for me." That generosity is easy to mistake for demand.

Now I try to look for evidence that someone has already tried to solve the problem themselves. A spreadsheet held together with formulas nobody understands. A Zapier automation. A recurring calendar reminder. Somebody paying a contractor to do it manually. Those workarounds are expensive and awkward and they exist anyway, which tells you the pain is worth money. Nobody builds a workaround for a problem they don't have.

We eventually killed the dashboard builder and replaced it with a weekly email showing four metrics with an arrow next to each one. It took a sprint. Open rates sit around 60% and it comes up in sales calls constantly.

The lesson I keep relearning is that requests tell you where people are looking, not what they will do. The gap between those two things is where roadmaps go to die.

If you're about to commit a quarter to something, one question worth sitting with: what is the customer doing today instead, and how much does it actually cost them? If you can't answer that with specifics, you probably aren't ready to build yet.

I wasn't. Four months taught me that better than any framework could have.
=== END OF TEXT A ===

=== TEXT B ===
**We spent four months building a feature. Six people used it.**

Not six percent. Six people. Out of about 4,000 weekly active accounts.

The feature was a custom dashboard builder. Drag your own widgets, pick your own metrics, save your own views. It came up in nearly every enterprise sales call. It was the third-most-requested item in our feedback tool. Three engineers and a designer worked on it for a full quarter.

We shipped it on a Thursday. I posted about it in the company Slack with a rocket emoji.

By the following month, adoption had flatlined at 0.4%. Retention among the people who *did* build a dashboard was worse than average — they'd build one, never open it again, and go back to the default view.

Here's what I got wrong, and it wasn't a prioritization problem. It was a listening problem.

Customers weren't asking for a dashboard builder. They were telling me they didn't trust our numbers.

When someone said "I want to build my own view," what they meant was: "Your default report shows a number my CFO doesn't recognize, and I can't figure out how you calculated it, so I export to a spreadsheet and rebuild it myself." The request was a workaround they'd invented for a problem they didn't have the language for. I took the workaround at face value and built it faster and prettier.

The fix, when we finally found it, was a definitions panel. Click any metric, see exactly how it's computed, which filters apply, and what's excluded. Two engineers, three weeks. Spreadsheet exports dropped 60%. Nobody ever asked us for a definitions panel.

Three things I do differently now:

**I ask about the last time, not the next time.** "Would you use this?" gets you politeness. "Walk me through the last time you needed this — what did you actually do?" gets you the truth, including the ugly workaround that reveals the real problem.

**I write down what would make us wrong.** Before we build, we agree on a number: if fewer than X% of eligible accounts use this in 30 days, we were wrong about the problem, and we run a retro instead of a victory lap. Having that number in writing beforehand makes it much harder to quietly redefine success afterward.

**I separate demand from evidence.** A feature request is a signal that something hurts. It is not a diagnosis. Ten people asking for the same thing can still be ten people describing the same symptom of an entirely different disease.

The uncomfortable part: I don't think we were sloppy. We talked to customers. We looked at the data. We just mistook *volume of requests* for *understanding of the problem*, and those are not the same thing at all.

What's the feature you're proudest of killing?
=== END OF TEXT B ===

{"more_ai": "A" or "B", "confidence": 1-5, "tells_A": ["short tell", ...], "tells_B": ["short tell", ...]}

tells_B: repeated 'wasn't X. It was Y' parallelism
